promptText: Why can't a coding assistant simply send the entire codebase to the model on every request?
options: Context windows are finite and cost scales with input size; irrelevant files also dilute the model's attention on what matters, tending to reduce output quality even when everything technically fits
IDEs technically prevent more than one file from being uploaded at a time
Compilers cannot process more than one file per invocation
Retrieval indexes are physically limited to storing a single file each
explanation: Beyond a small toy project this is impossible or prohibitively slow and expensive, and dumping irrelevant files dilutes the model's attention on the current task even when the tokens technically fit.

promptText: What is "fill-in-the-middle" (FIM) training, and why does it matter for coding assistants?
options: A training objective where the model learns to generate a missing span given text both before and after it, matching how a developer's cursor sits in the middle of existing code rather than at the end of a prefix
A technique that automatically fills in missing import statements using static analysis alone
A method for compressing source code before it is embedded into a vector store
A specialized objective used only for generating unit tests, not general completions
explanation: A plain left-to-right model given only text before the cursor structurally cannot generate a completion consistent with code that already follows it; FIM training specifically teaches the model to fit a missing middle span.

promptText: What is the purpose of the "verification loop" (compile/lint/test) in an agentic coding assistant?
options: It converts the model's probabilistic, potentially hallucinated output into a pass/fail signal grounded in the project's real compiler and test suite, rather than trusting the model's own self-assessment
It counts how many tokens the model consumed during generation
It automatically merges an approved pull request into the main branch
It replaces the need to show the developer a diff before applying changes
explanation: "I've verified this compiles" from a model is a claim about plausible text, not a fact - only an actual build/test run is ground truth, which is why this is the single most important step in the pipeline.

promptText: Why does inline code completion typically use a smaller, faster model than chat mode in the same product?
options: Completions fire on nearly every pause in typing and need sub-second responses, and are requested far more often per developer than chat messages, making a large model prohibitively slow and costly at that volume
Smaller models are always more accurate at generating code than larger ones
Chat mode does not use a language model at all, only inline completion does
Inline completions never need to be recomputed once cached, so model size is irrelevant
explanation: Two forces push toward a smaller model: sub-second latency requirements and the sheer volume of completion requests per developer per day compared to chat messages.

promptText: What does "sandboxed execution" protect against in a coding assistant with tool access?
options: Running model-proposed builds or tests inside an isolated environment with no production credentials or network reachability, so an unverified or injected command cannot cause real damage
It prevents the developer's IDE from crashing whenever a syntax error occurs
It hides the source code from the model entirely during generation
It guarantees that any code the model generates will compile successfully
explanation: Whether a bad command comes from a genuine misunderstanding or an injected instruction, sandboxing contains its blast radius before the code has been verified.

promptText: Why is code retrieval described as harder than plain-text RAG document retrieval?
options: Code relevance often depends on structural relationships - imports, call graphs, type hierarchies - that can make the single most relevant file textually dissimilar to the query, which pure embedding similarity misses
Source code files are always physically larger than prose documents
Code cannot be converted into vector embeddings using the same techniques as text
Compilers block retrieval systems from reading source files during indexing
explanation: A file can be the single most relevant piece of context (e.g., a class being directly called) while being textually dissimilar to the query, so production systems combine vector similarity with a structural symbol graph.

promptText: In the agentic edit pipeline, why does the model produce changes as a diff/patch rather than regenerating the whole file?
options: Diffs keep changes reviewable, leave unrelated code untouched, and reduce the risk of the model "forgetting" code that exists outside its immediate attention window
No LLM API is currently capable of returning more than one file in a single response
Diffs are required because compilers refuse to parse a fully regenerated file
Patch application always executes faster at runtime than a compiled full file
explanation: Targeted edits keep changes small and reviewable and dramatically reduce the chance of the model silently dropping code that existed outside its immediate attention.

promptText: What role does a symbol/dependency graph, built from the compiler or language server, play alongside vector embeddings in code retrieval?
options: It captures structural relationships embeddings alone cannot see, guaranteeing structurally necessary code - such as the actual definition being called - is retrieved even when it is textually dissimilar to the query
It fully replaces the need for any LLM call in the retrieval pipeline
It is used only in inline-completion mode and never in chat or agentic edits
It exists solely to store embeddings more compactly on disk
explanation: Embeddings surface semantically related code, while the graph guarantees structurally necessary code (the actual definition being called) is never missed, since production retrieval combines both signals.

promptText: Why should self-correction retry loops in an agentic coding assistant be explicitly bounded (e.g., 3-5 cycles)?
options: An unbounded loop can burn unbounded tokens chasing a task the model fundamentally cannot solve; a bounded loop must instead surface a clear failure state with the last error attached to the developer
Compilers physically refuse to run more than five times in a single session
IDEs are hard-coded to crash after exactly three failed build attempts
Bounded loops are a requirement imposed by the fill-in-the-middle training objective
explanation: A pipeline with no retry cap can burn unbounded tokens chasing a task the model cannot solve, while a pipeline with a cap can fail informatively with the failing test output attached.

promptText: What is "slopsquatting," and why is it a security concern for coding assistants specifically?
options: An attacker publishes a real, malicious package under a plausible-sounding name that an LLM is statistically likely to hallucinate as a dependency, so a suggested import can lead a developer to install attacker-controlled code
A technique for automatically compressing sloppy, unformatted code before a commit
A method attackers use specifically to slow down continuous-integration pipelines
A vulnerability that only affects models trained with a fill-in-the-middle objective
explanation: Dependency additions proposed by an assistant should be validated against a real package registry and an internal allowlist before being accepted, precisely because of this documented attack pattern.

promptText: Why is a language server (LSP) integration valuable to a coding assistant beyond what the LLM alone can provide?
options: It grounds suggestions in verified, ground-truth facts - the compiler's actual resolved type or method signature - rather than the model's statistical guess about a similarly-named symbol
It fully replaces the need for a vector store or symbol graph in the pipeline
It automatically executes the generated code to check for runtime errors
It converts the entire codebase into training data for future fine-tuning runs
explanation: Framing this as "grounding vs. guessing" is the key distinction: LSP integration is one of the cheapest, highest-leverage ways to inject deterministic ground truth before it ever reaches the model.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend AST-aware chunking over fixed-size chunking when indexing a codebase for retrieval?
options: Fixed-size chunking can slice a function or class definition in half, while AST-aware chunking splits along syntactic boundaries so each retrieved chunk remains a complete, coherent unit
AST-aware chunking is always computationally cheaper than fixed-size chunking regardless of file size
Fixed-size chunking cannot produce output that is compatible with vector embeddings
AST-aware chunking removes the need to maintain a separate symbol/dependency graph
explanation: Chunking along syntactic boundaries - a whole function, class, or method - ensures every retrieved chunk is a complete unit the model can actually reason about, instead of a fragment missing its signature or closing brace.

promptText: A developer reports the assistant keeps suggesting a method that doesn't exist on their service class. Which of the following is NOT one of the chapter's likely root causes or fixes for this specific failure?
options: Switching the assistant's output mode from streaming to non-streaming
The actual class definition was never retrieved into context - fix by prioritizing symbol-graph relevance over pure semantic similarity
The repo index is stale after a recent rename or refactor - fix with incremental re-indexing on save or commit
The model is pattern-matching a similarly-named method from public training data - mitigate with stronger system-prompt constraints and the verification loop's compile-error feedback
explanation: Streaming versus non-streaming output is unrelated to hallucinated methods; the chapter's actual diagnosis covers missed retrieval, a stale index, and pattern-matched hallucination from training data.

promptText: An organization wants to let the coding assistant auto-apply "small, safe" changes without human review. What is the chapter's staff-level assessment of the core flaw, and the better alternative?
options: "Safe" is being judged by the model's own confidence or by superficial diff size, neither a calibrated correctness signal; the better approach is a graduated trust model permitting auto-apply only for a narrow, empirically validated category (full build+test pass, no external callers per the symbol graph) with full audit logging and easy rollback
There is no flaw in the framing - diff size is a reliable, calibrated proxy for correctness, so broad auto-apply should be enabled immediately
Auto-apply should never be considered under any circumstances, even after an extensive human-reviewed pilot
The real flaw is that auto-apply is technically infeasible without direct production database credentials
explanation: The strongest answer rejects treating safety as a static property of a diff and reframes it as an empirical, measured trust boundary earned with pilot data and bounded by reversibility.

promptText: Which pair of signals does the chapter identify as a better indicator of AI-suggestion quality than raw acceptance rate alone?
options: Post-acceptance edit distance (how much of an accepted suggestion the developer immediately rewrites) and rollback/revert rate shortly after merge
Total number of tokens generated per session and time-to-first-token latency
Number of files the developer has open and the visual theme of their IDE
Total lines of code suggested compared to total characters typed by the developer
explanation: A high accept rate paired with high churn actually indicates the suggestion wasn't very good, just good enough to save some typing; churn and revert-rate get closer to measuring genuine correctness.
